lead: Crystallization makes a pure solid from a solution in one step: sugar from syrup, salt from brine, fertilisers, most drugs. A crystal grows only from a solution that holds more solute than it can hold at equilibrium, so the solubility curve says how much product can be won and supersaturation says how fast it forms.

blocks.text: A crystal is a solid whose atoms, ions or molecules are packed in a repeating three-dimensional lattice. Because the pattern repeats, a crystal is bounded by flat faces meeting at fixed angles, and the angles between corresponding faces are the same in every crystal of a substance. Crystals are sorted by the symmetry of their lattice into seven crystal systems: cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, triclinic, trigonal and hexagonal. Sodium chloride is cubic; sucrose is monoclinic.

The habit is the outward shape, needles, plates or blocks. One system can give several habits, because the relative growth rates of the faces change with solvent, supersaturation and impurities: sodium chloride grows as cubes from pure water but as octahedra with a little urea present. Habit matters to the plant, since needles break and filter slowly while compact crystals wash and flow well. Some substances also form more than one lattice, called polymorphs (calcite and aragonite are both CaCO3); for drugs the polymorph sets solubility and must be controlled.

A crystal's size is given by one characteristic length L, usually the sieve opening it just passes. Its volume and surface are then k<sub>v</sub>L³ and k<sub>a</sub>L², with shape factors k<sub>v</sub> = 1, k<sub>a</sub> = 6 for a cube and k<sub>v</sub> = π/6, k<sub>a</sub> = π for a sphere.

Solubility is the concentration of a saturated solution, one in equilibrium with the solid. It is quoted per 100 parts of solvent (g per 100 g water) so that it does not change as solute leaves, and it depends mainly on temperature. The plot of solubility against temperature is the solubility curve. Most salts, such as KNO3, are much more soluble hot, so cooling crystallizes them. Sodium chloride hardly changes with temperature, so it is crystallized by evaporating water. A few salts, such as anhydrous Na2SO4 above 32.4 °C, are less soluble hot (inverse solubility) and deposit as scale on hot surfaces.

Many salts crystallize as hydrates, with water inside the lattice: Na2SO4·10H2O below 32.4 °C, MgSO4·7H2O, CuSO4·5H2O. Each hydrate has its own branch of the curve, and the break at which one form changes into another is a transition point. For a solution of one salt in water the full diagram also shows the ice line, meeting the solubility curve at the eutectic, below which ice and salt freeze out together.
ΔC = C − C*      S = C/C*      σ = S − 1 = ΔC/C*
blocks.where: C is the actual concentration and C* the solubility at the same temperature, both in the same units. ΔC is the concentration driving force, S the supersaturation ratio and σ the relative supersaturation. A saturated solution has S = 1, σ = 0.

blocks.text: Miers found that a clean solution can be cooled below its saturation temperature without crystals appearing. Above the solubility curve there is a metastable zone, where existing crystals grow but new ones hardly form, and beyond the supersolubility curve a labile zone, where nuclei appear on their own. The supersolubility curve is not a fixed line like the solubility curve: it depends on the cooling rate, agitation and impurities. Good crystallizers run inside the metastable zone with seed crystals, so the solute goes onto growing crystals instead of forming showers of fines.

Supersaturation is created in four ways: by cooling a solution whose solubility falls with temperature; by evaporating solvent; by adding a second solvent or a salt that lowers the solubility (antisolvent or salting-out crystallization); and by a reaction that forms a sparingly soluble product (precipitation). Vacuum crystallization combines the first two: the feed boils at low pressure, and the evaporation both removes solvent and cools the solution.
With an ideal stage, the mother liquor leaves saturated at the final temperature. The balances are on total mass, solute and water:
F = P + M + V      solute: F x<sub>F</sub> = P x<sub>P</sub> + M s/(100 + s)
blocks.where: F feed, P crystals, M mother liquor, V water evaporated (kg). x<sub>F</sub> is the mass fraction of solute in the feed; x<sub>P</sub> is the mass fraction of anhydrous solute in the crystals (1 for anhydrous crystals, M<sub>salt</sub>/M<sub>hydrate</sub> for a hydrate); s is the final solubility in g per 100 g water. The water balance closes the set.

blocks.text: Evaporation and hydrate formation both raise the yield, because they leave less water to hold solute in the mother liquor. Real yields are lower if the mother liquor leaves still supersaturated.

examples.question: A salt has a solubility of 40 g per 100 g water at 60 °C and 20 g per 100 g water at 20 °C. 1000 kg of solution saturated at 60 °C is cooled to 20 °C. The crystals are anhydrous. Find the crystals formed and the yield (a) with no evaporation, (b) if 100 kg of water evaporates during cooling. (c) What is S when the solution first reaches 20 °C, before crystals form?
steps: (a) Water stays 714.3 kg; the mother liquor holds 714.3 × 20/100 = 142.9 kg of solute. Crystals = 285.7 − 142.9 = 142.9 kg; yield = 142.9/285.7 = 50.0 %.
Balance check for (b): crystals 162.9 + mother liquor (614.3 + 122.9 = 737.1) + vapour 100 = 1000 kg.

(c) The cooled solution still holds 40 g per 100 g water where 20 g is the solubility: S = 40/20 = 2.0, σ = 1.0, far into the labile zone, which is why uncontrolled cooling gives a shower of fine crystals.
examples.answer: 142.9 kg of crystals (50 %) without evaporation; 162.9 kg (57 %) with 100 kg evaporated; S = 2.0 if no crystals have formed by 20 °C.

examples.question: 1000 kg of a magnesium sulfate solution holding 40 g MgSO<sub>4</sub> per 100 g water is cooled until the solubility is 25 g per 100 g water. The crystals are MgSO<sub>4</sub>·7H<sub>2</sub>O (MgSO<sub>4</sub> 120.37, H<sub>2</sub>O 18.015). Find the crystals formed and the yield, and compare with anhydrous crystals at the same solubility.
steps: Feed: MgSO<sub>4</sub> = 285.7 kg; water = 714.3 kg. Hydrate molar mass = 120.37 + 7 × 18.015 = 246.48, so the crystals are 120.37/246.48 = 0.4884 MgSO<sub>4</sub> and 0.5116 water.
Let H be the hydrate formed. Water left in mother liquor = 714.3 − 0.5116H; MgSO<sub>4</sub> left = 0.25(714.3 − 0.5116H).
MgSO<sub>4</sub> in crystals = 0.4884 × 297.2 = 145.2 kg; yield = 145.2/285.7 = 50.8 %. Check: mother liquor 702.8 kg holds 140.6 kg MgSO<sub>4</sub> in 562.2 kg water, 25.0 g per 100 g.
Anhydrous at the same solubility: 285.7 − 0.25 × 714.3 = 107.1 kg, yield 37.5 %. The 152 kg of water locked in the hydrate leaves less water to hold salt.
examples.answer: 297.2 kg of MgSO<sub>4</sub>·7H<sub>2</sub>O carrying 145.2 kg of MgSO<sub>4</sub> (50.8 % yield), against 107.1 kg (37.5 %) if the crystals were anhydrous.

traps: Solubility in g per 100 g water is per 100 g of water, not per 100 g of solution: 40 g/100 g water is 28.6 mass% solute.
For a hydrate, the crystals carry water away from the mother liquor; leaving out that water underestimates the yield.
The supersolubility curve is not a property like the solubility curve; it moves with cooling rate, stirring and impurities.
S = C/C* and σ = S − 1 are different: a solution with S = 1.5 has σ = 0.5.

quiz.a: Cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, triclinic, trigonal (rhombohedral) and hexagonal.

quiz.q: Distinguish crystal system and crystal habit, with an example.
quiz.a: The system is the symmetry of the lattice and is fixed for a substance; the habit is the outward shape, which changes with growth conditions. NaCl is always cubic in system but grows as cubes from water and as octahedra with urea present.

quiz.q: A solution holds 45 g per 100 g water where the solubility is 30 g per 100 g water. Find ΔC, S and σ.
Explain the metastable and labile zones of Miers' supersaturation theory.
quiz.a: Just above the solubility curve, in the metastable zone, crystals present will grow but new nuclei rarely form. Beyond the supersolubility curve, in the labile zone, nuclei form spontaneously. Seeded crystallizers work in the metastable zone to grow large crystals.

quiz.q: A solution of KNO<sub>3</sub> in 500 kg of water, saturated at 60 °C (110 g per 100 g water), is cooled to 20 °C (32 g per 100 g water). Find the crystals.
quiz.a: The solution holds 550 kg KNO<sub>3</sub> in 500 kg water; at 20 °C the water holds 160 kg. Crystals = 550 − 160 = 390 kg (yield 70.9 %).

quiz.q: Why is NaCl crystallized by evaporation and KNO<sub>3</sub> by cooling?
quiz.a: NaCl's solubility changes little with temperature (about 36–39 g per 100 g water from 20 to 100 °C), so cooling gives almost nothing and water must be removed. KNO<sub>3</sub>'s solubility falls more than threefold between 60 and 20 °C, so cooling alone gives a high yield.

beyond: Not for the exam. Plants now track supersaturation directly with probes in the crystallizer: infrared spectroscopy for the solution concentration and laser backscattering for the crystal count, so the cooling can be steered to stay inside the metastable zone. In medicines, polymorph screening is a regulatory step. Search for metastable zone width measurement and polymorph screening.

figure.caption: The worked example on the solubility diagram. The feed saturated at 60 °C (A) cools at constant composition; without crystals it would reach B at 20 °C with S = 2.0, deep in the labile zone. Crystallization brings the liquor down to the solubility curve at C, releasing 142.9 kg of crystals per 1000 kg of feed. The supersolubility curve (sketched) is not fixed; seeding keeps the path in the metastable zone.

spec.aria: Solubility in grams per 100 grams of water against temperature, rising from 20 at 20 degrees to 40 at 60 degrees, with a dashed supersolubility curve above it and the labile and metastable zones shaded; a horizontal arrow from the feed point at 60 degrees to point B at 20 degrees, then a dashed drop to the mother liquor point C on the curve.
